title: High Intellect Can Be a Barrier to Learning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article presents a paradox: highly intelligent leaders often struggle to learn precisely because their capability breeds overconfidence, which narrows curiosity and openness. It also notes that high-intellect people often need strong stimulation to stay engaged, so they learn voraciously in areas that interest them while shutting down inquiry elsewhere — a selective learning pattern that leaves gaps in exactly the areas they'll need in the future. The piece's prescription is behavioral: practice saying 'I don't know,' and deliberately explore topics that aren't inherently interesting, since intellect is only a learning asset when actively deployed.
points: The mechanism isn't lack of capacity but overconfidence: high intellect breeds the assumption of already knowing enough, which reduces openness to new input.
Selective engagement is identified as a hidden risk — smart people learn voraciously where interested and disengage elsewhere, leaving blind spots exactly where future needs will emerge.
The practical fix is behavioral discipline (deliberately practicing 'I don't know' and exploring uninteresting topics), not raw ability, since intellect only functions as a learning asset when used.
quotes: Here’s a paradox: The smarter a leader is, the more likely they will eventually have troubling learning.
But those with high intellect and aptitude sometimes become overconfident in what they know. This reduces their openness, curiosity, and inquiry, which severely limits their ability to learn.
This selective learning hides the fact that they are most comfortable with understanding what is relevant in the moment but not what they need to know in the future.
Remaining open, curious, and receptive to learning is not easy for anyone with deep experience and expertise, but it is even more difficult for leaders who are tremendously smart.
But most of all, impress upon them that the more they know, the more there is to learn.
